o: We must delete the whole array, where each move removes one contiguous palindromic chunk of the *current* array. Since removals merge neighbors, the state that matters is a subarray of the original array: after some sequence of moves, what remains is always a set of original segments glued together. So we think in terms of intervals. For example 1, [1,2] has no multi-element palindrome, so we pay 1 per element = 2. In example 2, [1,3,4,1,5]: remove [4] (move 1), then [1,3,1] is a palindrome (move 2), then [5] (move 3). With n ≤ 100, an O(n^3) interval DP over all (i, j) pairs is easily fast enough.
k: Any interleaving of removals can be reordered so each move deletes elements forming one contiguous segment of the original array, so interval DP over original indices is valid.
Key recurrence trick: if arr[i] == arr[k] for k > i, deleting arr[i+1..k-1] first merges arr[i] and arr[k] into one palindrome piece, giving dp[i][j] = min(dp[i+1][k-1] + dp[k+1][j]).
Base cases: single element costs 1; dp on empty ranges costs 0.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force recursion with memoization (top-down)
a.i: Define f(i, j) = minimum moves to clear arr[i..j]. Either remove arr[i] alone plus f(i+1, j), or if arr[i] == arr[k], remove arr[i+1..k-1] and arr[k] together with arr[i] as one palindrome move, then solve the rest. Memoize to avoid exponential blowup.
s: f(i, j) returns 0 for i > j and 1 for i == j.
Initialize best = 1 + f(i+1, j) (delete arr[i] alone).
For each k in (i+1..j) with arr[k] == arr[i], consider f(i+1, k-1) + f(k+1, j).
Memoize f(i, j) and return the minimum.
a.t: O(n^3) — O(n^2) states, each trying up to O(n) split points k.
a.sp: O(n^2) for the memo table plus O(n) recursion stack.

a.i: Same recurrence computed iteratively by increasing interval length. dp[i][j] = min moves to clear arr[i..j]. Transitions: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i+1][j]; and for every k with arr[i]==arr[k], dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], dp[i+1][k-1] + dp[k+1][j]). This is essentially the classic 'strange printer / burst balloons' family of interval DP.
s: Let n = len(arr); dp is n x n initialized to infinity.
Set dp[i][i] = 1 and dp[i][i-1] = 0 for all i.
For length L from 2 to n, for each start i (j = i + L - 1): set dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i+1][j].
For each k in (i+1..j) with arr[k] == arr[i], update dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], dp[i+1][k-1] + dp[k+1][j]).
a.t: O(n^3) — three nested loops over length, start, and split point; trivially fine for n ≤ 100.

w: In an interview, present the top-down formulation first to establish the recurrence, then code the bottom-up version since it avoids recursion overhead. Pitfalls: forgetting the empty-range base case (dp[i][i-1] = 0), forgetting the fallback transition dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i+1][j] when no matching partner exists, and assuming only exact palindromic substrings matter — the merging via equal endpoints is the crux. Edge cases: single element (answer 1), all-equal array (answer 1), strictly increasing array (answer n). Follow-ups: prove why greedy removal of the largest palindrome fails (e.g., [1,2,1,2,1]), or extend to counting maximum-length palindromic removals.
